question: According to the manual, why should a rider use their arms to steer rather than to hold themselves up on the motorcycle?
choice_a: Using arms to hold yourself up is actually the preferred technique
choice_b: Proper posture helps you bond with the motorcycle and react quickly to hazards
choice_c: Posture has no effect on control of the motorcycle
choice_d: Arms should be kept completely straight and rigid at all times
explanation: The manual explains that positioning yourself comfortably so you use your arms to steer, rather than to hold yourself up, helps you bond with the motorcycle and react quickly to hazards.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.11, 'Body Position'

question: Where should a rider sit on the seat, and why?
choice_a: As far back as possible to maximize leg room
choice_b: It does not matter where you sit as long as you can reach the ground
choice_c: Far enough forward so the arms are slightly bent when holding the handgrips, avoiding the need to stretch
choice_d: Perched on the very edge of the seat at all times
explanation: The manual instructs riders to sit far enough forward that the arms are slightly bent when holding the handgrips, which lets the rider press on the handlebars without having to stretch.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.11, 'Body Position'

question: How should a rider start their right wrist when gripping the handlebar, and why?
choice_a: Sharply bent upward, for maximum throttle control
choice_b: Wrist position makes no difference to throttle control
choice_c: Twisted fully open at all times while riding
choice_d: Flat, to help avoid accidentally using too much throttle
explanation: The manual advises starting with the right wrist flat, which helps prevent accidentally using too much throttle.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.11, 'Body Position'

question: Why does the manual say a rider should keep their knees against the gas tank?
choice_a: To help keep balance as the motorcycle turns
choice_b: To keep the tank warm in cold weather
choice_c: It is purely a matter of rider comfort with no control benefit
explanation: The manual states that keeping the knees against the gas tank helps the rider keep balance as the motorcycle turns.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.11, 'Body Position'

question: What does the manual warn about letting your toes point downward while riding?
choice_a: It improves aerodynamics at highway speed
choice_b: They may get caught between the road and the footrests
choice_c: It has no safety implication at all
choice_d: It is required technique for tight, slow turns
explanation: The manual warns that if toes point downward, they may get caught between the road and the footrests, which is why feet should be kept firmly on the footrests.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.11, 'Body Position'

question: How is the gearshift lever on a typical motorcycle operated?
choice_a: It is a hand lever on the right handlebar
choice_b: It is operated by the right foot only
choice_c: It is located in front of the left footrest and operated by the left foot -- lift to upshift, press down to downshift
choice_d: Shifting is done entirely with the throttle, with no separate lever
explanation: The manual explains the gearshift lever is located in front of the left footrest and operated by the left foot: lifting the lever shifts up to a higher gear, and pressing it down shifts down.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.11, 'Shifting Gears'

question: In a typical 1-N-2-3-4-5 gear pattern, how is neutral usually selected?
choice_a: By pulling the clutch lever all the way to the handgrip
choice_b: By turning off the ignition while in motion
choice_c: Neutral cannot be selected while the engine is running
choice_d: By a 'half lift' from first gear or a 'half press' from second gear
explanation: The manual states that in a typical gear pattern of 1-N-2-3-4-5, neutral is selected by either a 'half lift' from 1st gear or a 'half press' from 2nd gear.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.11-12, 'Shifting Gears'

question: What is the correct 3-step process for upshifting described in the manual?
choice_a: Roll off the throttle while squeezing the clutch, lift the shift lever firmly as far as it will go, then smoothly ease out the clutch and adjust the throttle
choice_b: Squeeze the clutch, apply the rear brake, then release both at the same time
choice_c: Roll on the throttle first, then worry about the clutch afterward
choice_d: Press the shift lever down firmly while accelerating hard
explanation: The manual's 3-step upshifting process is: 1) roll off the throttle as you squeeze the clutch lever, 2) lift the shift lever firmly as far as it will go, 3) smoothly ease out the clutch and adjust the throttle.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.12, 'Shifting Gears'

question: What technique does the manual describe as 'engine braking'?
choice_a: Using the front brake exclusively while in a high gear
choice_b: Shifting down one gear at a time and easing out the clutch through the friction zone between each downshift
choice_c: Turning off the engine to slow the motorcycle
choice_d: Riding in neutral down a long hill
explanation: The manual describes engine braking as shifting to a lower gear, which causes an effect similar to using the brakes; to use it, shift down one gear at a time and ease out the clutch through the friction zone between each downshift.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.12, 'Shifting Gears'

question: Why does the manual say a rider should remain in first gear while stopped?
choice_a: First gear keeps the engine cooler at idle
choice_b: It is required by law in most states
choice_c: So the rider can move out quickly if needed
choice_d: It has no particular purpose; any gear works equally well
explanation: The manual advises remaining in first gear while stopped so that you can move out quickly if you need to.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.12, 'Shifting Gears'

question: What does the manual say about shifting gears while already in a turn?
choice_a: Shifting gears mid-turn is always perfectly safe with no precautions needed
choice_b: Shifting is impossible while the motorcycle is leaned over
choice_c: Riders should always downshift aggressively mid-turn to add stability
choice_d: It is best to change gears before entering a turn, but if shifting in the turn is necessary, do so smoothly since a sudden power change can cause a skid
explanation: The manual advises changing gears before entering a turn when possible; if shifting while turning is necessary, it should be done smoothly, since a sudden change in power to the rear wheel can cause a skid.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.12, 'Shifting Gears'

question: What percentage of a motorcycle's total stopping power can the front brake provide?
choice_c: Exactly 25%, with the rear brake providing the rest
choice_d: 0%; the front brake should never be used
explanation: The manual states the front brake is more powerful and can provide at least 70% of a motorcycle's total stopping power, and is safe to use if used properly.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.13, 'Braking'

question: How should the front brake be applied during maximum straight-line braking?
choice_a: Grabbed hard and instantly to the maximum position
choice_b: Squeezed smoothly, firmly and with progressively more force, never grabbed or applied abruptly
choice_c: Applied only after the rear brake has fully stopped the motorcycle
choice_d: Never applied during an emergency stop
explanation: The manual instructs riders to squeeze the front brake smoothly, firmly and with progressively more force, and specifically not to grab the brake lever or use abrupt pressure.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.13, 'Braking'

question: As a motorcycle's weight transfers forward during braking, what happens to available traction at the front and rear wheels?
choice_a: Traction increases equally at both wheels
choice_b: Traction decreases at the front and increases at the rear
choice_c: More traction becomes available at the front wheel (allowing harder front braking), while less traction is available at the rear, requiring lighter rear brake pressure
choice_d: Weight transfer during braking has no effect on available traction
explanation: The manual explains that as the motorcycle's weight transfers forward, more traction becomes available at the front wheel, so the front brake can be applied harder; less traction is available at the rear, so lighter rear brake pressure should be used to prevent a rear wheel skid.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.13, 'Braking'

question: What does a linked braking system do, and how does an integrated braking system differ from it?
choice_a: Linked and integrated braking systems are identical in every respect
choice_b: A linked system disables the rear brake completely
choice_c: An integrated system only functions above highway speeds
choice_d: A linked system applies braking pressure to both brakes when either the front lever or rear pedal is used; an integrated system applies partial front braking whenever the rear brake is activated
explanation: The manual explains that linked braking connects the front and rear brakes so that applying either the front lever or rear pedal applies both; an integrated braking system is a variation in which partial front braking is applied whenever the rear brake is activated.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.13, 'Linked and Integrated Braking Systems'

question: What is the purpose of an Anti-Lock Braking System (ABS), and how many times per second can it release and reapply pressure?
choice_a: It prevents wheel lock-up and skids during straight-line panic stops, and can release and reapply pressure more than 15 times per second
choice_b: It is designed only to improve fuel economy
choice_c: It works only when riding below 5 mph
choice_d: It replaces the need for both the front and rear brake levers
explanation: The manual states ABS is designed to prevent wheel lock-up and avoid skids when stopping in straight-line, panic situations, activating when maximum pressure is applied to both brake controls, and is capable of releasing and reapplying pressure more than 15 times per second.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.13, 'Anti-Lock Braking Systems (ABS)'

question: What are the manual's four steps for better control through a turn?
choice_b: SLOW (reduce speed before the turn), LOOK (through the turn to where you want to go), PRESS (on the handgrip in the turn direction to lean), and ROLL (on the throttle to maintain or slightly increase speed)
choice_d: There are no defined steps; each rider improvises
explanation: The manual's four steps for better control through a turn are SLOW, LOOK, PRESS, and ROLL -- reducing speed before the turn, looking through the turn, pressing the handgrip in the direction of the turn to lean, and rolling on the throttle to stabilize the motorcycle.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.14, 'Turning'

question: When looking through a turn, what does the manual say a rider should turn -- and what should stay level?
choice_a: Turn your entire upper body including your shoulders as far as possible
choice_b: Keep your head perfectly still and only move your eyes
choice_c: Turn just your head, not your shoulders, and keep your eyes level with the horizon
choice_d: Tilt your head to match the lean angle of the motorcycle
explanation: The manual instructs riders to turn just the head, not the shoulders, and to keep the eyes level with the horizon while looking through a turn.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.14, 'Turning'

question: In slow, tight turns, how should a rider counterbalance compared to a normal turn?
choice_a: By leaning the body further than the motorcycle in every turn
choice_b: Counterbalancing technique is identical for slow and normal-speed turns
choice_c: By keeping both feet off the footrests for balance
choice_d: By leaning the motorcycle only and keeping the body straight, rather than leaning the body and motorcycle together
explanation: The manual explains that in normal turns, the rider and motorcycle lean together at the same angle, but in slow, tight turns, the rider should counterbalance by leaning the motorcycle only and keeping the body straight.
source_note: MS Motorcycle Operator Manual (MSF 17th Ed.), p.14, 'Turning'
